turns.prompt_text: How difficult is it to pick a lot? I've tried a few times and it seems I'm really bad at it I wonder how people figured out how to do it
turns.response_html:
It is completely normal to struggle with lock picking initially—you aren't bad at it, it’s just an entirely blind, tactile skill. It forces you to rely on feedback that your hands usually ignore, like the micro-vibrations of a tiny piece of metal scraping against brass.

The breakthrough moment for lock picking historically came down to a fundamental truth of engineering: nothing is perfectly manufactured.

The Flaw That Makes It Possible

If every lock were physically perfect, picking a standard pin-tumbler lock would be nearly impossible.

In a perfect lock, all the pin holes would be drilled in a perfectly straight line through the center of the cylinder. When you applied rotational tension, every single pin would bind at the exact same fraction of a millimeter.

Because of microscopic manufacturing imperfections, those pin holes are always slightly out of alignment.

When you apply light rotational force with a tension wrench, the cylinder rotates just a tiny fraction of a degree until it hits just one driver pin. That specific pin binds first because its hole is slightly off-center compared to the others.

How People Figured It Out

Early locks (like ancient Egyptian wooden locks or medieval warded locks) relied on physical obstructions. If you could shape a piece of metal to bypass the obstacles and grab the bolt, it opened.

But when Linus Yale Sr. and his son revolutionized the modern pin-tumbler lock in the mid-1800s, it seemed unpickable because the mechanism was hidden deep inside a solid metal plug. Locksmiths and curious engineers figured out how to beat it by studying physics and tolerances:

  1. The Binding Principle: They realized that under tension, the pins don't all resist equally. By feeling for the one pin that is stiff and resisting movement (the binding pin), they could lift it until the gap between the key pin and driver pin aligned perfectly with the shear line (the gap where the inner cylinder turns inside the outer housing).
  2. The "Click": When that driver pin clears the shear line, the cylinder rotates an invisible hair further until it catches on the next worst-machined pin hole. This creates a tiny tactile click or drop that you can feel through your tension wrench.

Why You're Having a Hard Time

If you're stuck, it almost always comes down to tension control.

Beginners tend to use way too much force on the tension wrench. When you press too hard, you bind multiple pins simultaneously, locking them in place so tightly that you can't lift them cleanly, or you push them past the shear line into an "over-set" state where they trap the cylinder completely.

The Golden Rule: You only want enough tension to feel resistance. If you are pressing hard enough to turn your finger white, it's too much. Imagine the pressure it takes to hold a single sheet of paper against a wall without letting it fall—that's usually all it takes.

Learning it is essentially teaching your brain a new sensory language. It takes time to separate the feeling of a pin just springy-sliding vs. a pin actually binding.

turns.prompt_text: One big issue with this is I don't know if I have the correct tools I've seen. I've heard about using a paper clip and a bobby pin or maybe like a thread needle, but I'm not sure what would actually work except for buying the really expensive professional tools
turns.response_html:
You absolutely do not need expensive professional toolsets to get started, but improvising with household items like paperclips or sewing needles is a massive uphill battle. Those makeshift tools flex too much, don't transmit tactile feedback well, and often can't get the leverage you need.

Before you give up on the hobby, there is a middle ground between "useless paperclips" and "pricey pro kits."

The Two Tools You Actually Need

To pick a lock, you only ever need two basic implements. Anything more is just extra fluff for specialized locks.

  1. The Tension Wrench: This is the most critical tool. It applies the light rotational force needed to catch the binding pins.
  2. The Pick: This is used to manipulate individual pins inside the cylinder. A standard Hook pick or a City Rake is all you need for 90% of beginner locks.

Highly Effective, Low-Cost Options

You can get high-quality, professional-grade tools for less than the cost of a fast-casual lunch. You don't need a 30-piece kit; you just need two or three good individual pieces.

1. The Budget Pro Route (Under $15)

Instead of buying massive kits, buy individual tools ("singles") from reputable locksmith supply or locksport sites (like Sparrows Lock Picks, SouthOrd, or Covert Instruments).

  • A standard short hook pick usually costs around $4 to $5.
  • A couple of basic tension wrenches cost about $2 to $3 each.
  • For around $10–$15 total, you will have the exact same high-quality, spring-steel tools that professionals use, without paying for a giant carrying case full of filler tools you'll never touch.

2. The DIY Windshield Wiper Trick (Free to $2)

If you love the maker approach and want to build your own high-quality tools, don't use bobby pins. Go to an auto parts store (or look in a dumpster) for an old windshield wiper blade.

Inside the rubber squeegee of almost every standard wiper blade is a thin, flat strip of high-tensile stainless steel.

  • For a tension wrench: Snap off a 3-inch piece of this steel inserts, bend it at a 90-degree angle on one end using a pair of pliers, and you have a tension tool that is arguably better than many cheap retail versions.
  • For a pick: You can use a small file, a Dremel tool, or a bench grinder to carefully shape the tip of another strip into a small hook. Because wiper blade steel is designed to resist bending, it transmits the tactile vibrations of the pins beautifully.

Why Paperclips and Bobby Pins Fail

If you've been struggling with paperclips, give yourself some grace—they are actively working against you.

Paperclips are made of soft, low-carbon steel. When you push up on a binding pin, the paperclip simply bends inside the lock instead of moving the pin. You can't feel the "click" because the metal absorbs all the vibration. Bobby pins are made of better steel, but they are typically too thick to fit into a standard keyway without dragging against the walls, which completely masks the subtle feelings of the pins shifting.

A proper tool made of thin, rigid spring steel makes it a completely different experience. You will instantly start feeling the feedback you've been missing.

turns.prompt_text: Yes and can I pick them up locally?
turns.response_html:
Unfortunately, finding dedicated lock picks in a brick-and-mortar retail store is nearly impossible. Because it is such a niche hobby and because of the general stigma around "burglary tools," standard brick-and-mortar hardware stores do not stock actual lock-picking kits on their shelves.

If you see a "Hook and Pick Set" at a local hardware store (like Harbor Freight, Home Depot, or Ace Hardware), those are actually automotive and mechanical tools meant for pulling rubber O-rings, cotter pins, and hoses. They are way too thick and shaped incorrectly to fit inside a keyway.

However, you can source the materials to make or practice with them locally right now, or order exactly what you need online for very little money.

What to Pick Up Locally Today

If you want to go the immediate, local DIY route, you can get everything you need with a quick trip to an auto parts or local hardware store:

  • Windshield Wiper Blades (Free to $5): Stop by a local auto parts store. If you ask the staff nicely if they have any old, snapped wiper blades they just replaced and threw in the trash, they will usually hand them over for free. Pull out the metal insert strip to make your tension wrench and pick.
  • A Small File or Bench Grinder ($2 - $15): A local hardware store will have a cheap set of needle files or a small hand file to shape the tip of your wiper blade steel into a perfect hook.
  • A Cheap Padlock ($5 - $10): While you're at the hardware store, grab a basic, cheap Master Lock (like a Master Lock No. 1, No. 3, or No. 140). Avoid high-end brands like Schlage or American Lock for now. Cheap locks have terrible manufacturing tolerances, which ironically makes them the absolute best for learning because the "binding" pins are incredibly obvious.

The Ideal Mini-Kit to Buy Online (Under $15)

If you decide to just buy the proper tools online, skip the massive kits and buy individual pieces from highly respected locksport sites like Sparrows Lock Picks or Covert Instruments.

The perfect minimalist setup consists of just three items:

  1. A Standard Short Hook (0.025" or 0.020" thickness): This is the definitive, quintessential profile used to feel and lift individual pins. (Cost: ~$4.50)
  2. A "City Rake" or "B-Rake": Raking is a different technique where you gently scrub the pick across all the pins at once to bounce them into place. It’s a great confidence booster because it opens cheap padlocks in seconds. (Cost: ~$4.50)
  3. A Few Flatbar/Z-bar Tension Wrenches: Grab a small pack of standard bottom-of-the-keyway (BOK) or top-of-the-keyway (TOK) tension bars. (Cost: ~$3.00)

Ordering these few singles will give you genuine, professional-grade spring steel that won't bend out of shape, handles beautifully, and keeps your total cost under fifteen bucks.
